newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Making room at top in S.Africa's "rainbow" Reserve Bank.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Making room at top in S.Africa's "rainbow" Reserve Bank.

text.p: One floor below the penthouse office of Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals sits the man who has begun dismantling an edifice that until recently served as a bastion for white South African males.

Armed with the mantras of "tranformation in terms of ethnicity and gender" and "excellence with diversity" he has set about rebuilding the central bank to reflect the realities of post-apartheid South Africa's "rainbow" society of many colours.
Over the last 10 months, deputy governor Timothy Thahane says tangible progress has been made.
"When I came here I found a well-managed institution which could compare adequately with any in the world," said Thahane, one of Stals's three deputies.
"The part that was disappointing was that it was mainly white and mainly male," he told Reuters in an interview.

An effort to change its white image was initiated as far back as 1993 by the Reserve Bank, although Thahane says the focus at the time was on the lower echelons of bank personnel, and carried out at what he feels was a sedentary pace.
Since stepping in to accelerate reform, Thahane has focused on shifting the mindset among middle and senior management towards change -- an effort he says has borne fruit.
NECESSITY FOR CHANGE ACCEPTED

"Over the last 10 months, the basic achievement has been an acceptance by all the managers and staff of the necessity to change the bank's culture and transform it in terms of gender and ethnicity," he says.
In the years ahead, Thahane has set his sights on rebuilding the bank through the various programmes, such as attitudinal workshops, that he has introduced.
He is no stranger to building. To finance a high school education in his native Lesotho, he helped his father make bricks.
That led him to a university education in Canada where he completed a commerce degree, majoring in labour relations, and an economic masters in the late 1960s.

His professional career began with the Lesotho government where he worked in the economic planning department, focusing on economic development in the country and financing negotiations with multilateral and bilateral agencies.

He then spent the better part of the last 25 years in several senior positions in the World Bank, a profile which he says exposed him to policy decisions as well as the intricacies of loan financing and the financial markets.

From 1980, he worked as vice president and secretary of the World Bank, before joining South Africa's Reserve Bank in 1996 where he spearheaded, among other functions, its affirmative action programme.
His appointment as deputy governor in June last year coincided with rumours of current governor Chris Stals's imminent resignation, with Thahane whispered as his successor.

There are market commentators who continue to expect Thahane to be named as Stals's successor, although others point to the fact that he is Lesotho-born and has no extensive central bank experience as factors which preclude him taking residence in the office upstairs.
While Thahane's name is likely to be among those considered for the post, which becomes vacant in 1999, he is quick to dismiss speculation.
"The market and individuals are free to speculate but my response is that the government will make the decision on the best person to succeed Stals," he said.
For now, Thahane says he is committed to doing the best job he can in his present role.
REFORMS CAUSED UNEASE AMONG SENIOR STAFF
Thahane's aggressive pace has led to unease among some senior staff members, prompting some resignations with the prospect of more to come, according to insiders.
He acknowledges that but says these were not due soley to objections to reforms.
"There has been uncertainty and as the 'valuing diversity' workshops proceed, people understand what the objectives are and what contributions they can make.
"Clearly there may be people who may still have their reservations but they have not come out overtly to say that they are unhappy. We have found people willing to be a part of the transformation."
Thahane says his vision for the bank by the end of his tenure in 2001 is one that espouses a modern management philosophy.

"What I would like to see is a bank characterised by professional and technical excellence in diversity and a management culture that values diversity and encourages teamwork, coaching, mentoring of new staff and effective training in terms of skill development of management and human resources."

"If one looks to the future, excellence with diversity in terms of gender and ethnicity has to be done quickly in order to maintain the public trust that has been placed in the bank, otherwise that trust will soon be eroded," Thahane says.
